implementation_notes: Swift's Synchronization module supplies the guardian directly: `Mutex<Value>` is documented as a primitive that 'protects shared mutable state via mutual exclusion' and only one execution context at a time has access to the value stored within it, so `store.withLock { ... }` is the sole route to the state and the closure's result is the only thing that escapes. Before that type (or when the deployment target forbids it) the classic form is a class with private state and an `NSLock`/`os_unfair_lock` around each accessor - still justified for short synchronous sections. The language-level answer is stronger and is the reason this pattern is 'native' in Swift: an `actor` is 'an object that protects access to mutable data by forcing code to take turns accessing that data', enforced by the compiler, so shared reference types that must be touched from async code belong in an actor rather than behind a manual lock.
pitfalls: `NSLock` is not recursive: calling `lock()` from a method that already holds it self-deadlocks, and every `lock()` needs a matching `unlock()` on all paths (`Mutex.withLock` cannot leak).
Doing long work or calling out to other code inside `withLock` serialises every user of the cache; the closure should only touch the guarded value.

Mixing isolation models is the classic Swift error: `@MainActor` state must not be mutated from a background task even when a lock protects it, and an actor's state must not be reached by taking a lock around it - each guarantee is enforced by a different mechanism.

variants.name: Actor isolation
variants.implementation_notes: An `actor` is Swift's compiler-enforced guardian: its mutable state is isolated, and any access from outside must `await` the actor, which runs one piece of isolated code at a time - the swift-book formulation is that an actor protects access to mutable data by forcing code to take turns. Prefer it over a lock whenever the callers are async, when the state must be shared between tasks, or when an invariant spans several `await`-separated steps: the serialisation is checked statically instead of relying on a lock discipline. It costs a suspension at every cross-actor access, it is not a general purpose mutex (no `tryLock`, no blocking callers), and `nonisolated`/`Sendable` escapes must be designed deliberately.
pitfalls: Awaiting between read and write inside an actor method still lets other work interleave at the suspension point; a single isolated method must do the whole read-modify-write.
A reference type stored in an actor can still escape (returned, captured, or held by a `nonisolated` method), after which its state is unprotected - return values, not objects.
